bull_bear.body:
- Strong promoter brand: part of the Lalbhai Group, a professionally managed conglomerate with revenues exceeding USD 1.7 Bn and a legacy dating to 1897; the 'Arvind' name carries national recognition and, in an industry where trust decides home purchases, enhances customer confidence and premium positioning
- Promoter group holds 53.83% of ASL, with common directors across group companies providing strategic alignment and institutional support
- Lean, asset-light operating model: nearly 67% of projects are undertaken through joint development arrangements, enabling scalable growth with minimal capital intensity and a structurally lean fixed-cost base
- Strategic functions retained in-house while construction and execution are outsourced to specialised external partners, preserving oversight of planning, execution and quality

- Design-led approach and proven execution track record help secure high-quality joint development opportunities, partnerships and entry into new markets
- Diversified presence across Ahmedabad, Gandhinagar, Vadodara, Bengaluru, Pune and MMR, with FY25-26 expansion into MMR redevelopment (Santacruz, Goregaon) and a ~20 Mn sq ft township near Khopoli
- Customer advocacy: event-based Net Promoter Score improved from 55% to 61% and 10% of FY25-26 bookings came through loyalty and referrals
- Positioned to benefit from sector consolidation toward large, listed and branded developers, whose share of residential sales has risen steadily since FY16-17
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Workplace health, safety and labour-rights exposure at construction sites — Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk: 'The construction industry is prone to a high number of workplace injuries and accidents due to the nature of the work, which often involves heights and heavy machinery', with reputational risk if fair labour practices, human rights and employee health and safety are not ensured. Mitigation runs through the HIRA (Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment) framework, dedicated safety officers at active sites, regular training and tested emergency response plans; FY25-26 recorded a zero Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate, zero work-related injuries and zero fatalities. Because execution is largely outsourced to external contractors, the exposure sits partly outside direct control.
- Water availability and water-use regulation — Flagged in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk with negative financial implications: 'Considering our dependency on water for the viability of our operations, we have identified it as a material risk'. Non-compliance with water regulations can result in fines and legal issues, and poor water management can damage local ecosystems. Mitigation is designed in at the project stage — water-efficient construction materials that need less curing water, recycling, rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge.
- Emissions and energy management, including the risk of stricter future regulation — Flagged in the BRSR material-issues table with negative financial implications: high emissions and inefficient energy use raise operating costs, poor practices can damage brand value, buyers are shifting toward green construction so laggards 'may lose competitive advantage and market share', and 'long term strategic risks include the potential for stricter future regulations and the need for costly retrofits or upgrades to meet these new standards'.
- Rising leverage after a step-up in land and project investment — The Directors' Report records net borrowings of Rs. 31,302.96 Lakhs availed during the year, with investments in new lands and projects funded out of business inflows and incremental borrowings, and total standalone debt of Rs. 56,952.08 Lakhs as on March 31, 2026. Land and business-development spend is front-loaded relative to project cash realisation, so an aggressive acquisition pace makes the balance sheet more sensitive to a slowdown in bookings or collections.
- Dependence on a sustained new-launch cadence for bookings — New launches contributed nearly 60% of total FY26 bookings, approximately Rs. 930 Crores, and the two Q4 FY26 launches (Arvind Skycrest, Arvind Greenfields) drove a large share of the year's momentum. Bookings therefore depend on launches landing on schedule; approval, liaison or construction delays in a single large launch can move the whole year's pre-sales.
- Concentration of demand in the premium/mid-premium segment amid a softening mass market — The Directors' Report notes that homes above Rs. 1 crore rose to 63% of residential sales while 'demand in the sub-Rs. 1 crore segment softened noticeably', with premium housing at nearly 70% of new launches. The Company's mid-to-premium positioning aligns with the strong end of the market but concentrates exposure in the segment where developers are collectively adding the most supply, and leaves it exposed if the premiumisation trend reverses.
- Sensitivity to interest rates and housing affordability — Management attributes the favourable operating environment partly to 'improving affordability through lower interest rates' after 125 basis points of cumulative rate cuts and a repo rate of 5.25%. Housing demand and the Company's own borrowing cost both move with the rate cycle, so a reversal would compress buyer affordability and project economics simultaneously.
- Macro and capital-market volatility — The MD&A flags risks that 'persist, particularly from elevated energy prices, subsidy pressures on government spending, and uncertainty in global demand', alongside a 9.88% rupee depreciation in FY25-26 (the steepest since FY11-12), a record Rs. 1.8 Trn of FPI outflows, an 8% fall in India's market capitalisation and continued West Asia conflict. Global growth is projected to slow to 3.0% in 2026 with global inflation rising to 4.7%.
- Leadership transition and key-person dependence — The Board comprised ten Directors at the close of FY25-26 following substantial churn: Mr. Priyansh Kapoor was appointed Managing Director and CEO with effect from February 10, 2026 after the cessation of Mr. Kamal Singal, and the Chief Financial Officer position changed twice within roughly eighteen months. Management explicitly links the MMR pipeline's traction to the new MD's 'deep market networks and operating familiarity', which concentrates the newest growth platform on recently arrived leadership. Oversight is provided by a ten-member Board and seven committees, including a dedicated Risk Management Committee running enterprise-wide risk identification and mitigation.

business.body: Founded in 2008 in Ahmedabad as a wholly owned subsidiary of Arvind Limited and demerged in FY15-16, Arvind SmartSpaces develops residential, commercial and industrial real estate across key markets in Gujarat, Karnataka and Maharashtra. It is primarily focused on residential real estate for mid- and premium-income buyers through villas, apartments and plotted developments, with a portfolio centred on integrated townships that combine homes with executive golf courses, retail spaces, commercial centres and lifestyle amenities. Residential accounts for 93% of the ongoing and planned portfolio and commercial and industrial for 7%; within residential, 84% is mid-market, 14% premium and luxury and 2% affordable housing.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Build Mumbai/MMR into the next growth market: after entering redevelopment through Santacruz, the Company secured its largest property redevelopment opportunity in Goregaon in April 2026, deepening its long-term commitment to MMR, and will deepen presence through additional high-rise and redevelopment opportunities in FY26-27
- Scale across multiple cities so growth is no longer dependent on a single market — FY25-26 added projects across Bengaluru, Ahmedabad and Vadodara, diversifying the development pipeline
- Shift the portfolio mix toward group housing / high-rise alongside horizontal development: five of six FY25-26 acquisitions were high-rise residential, including re-entry into Ahmedabad's high-rise market after nearly a decade
- Increase the share of asset-light opportunities to enhance capital efficiency, alongside disciplined capital allocation and maintained investment return thresholds
- Institutionalise business development: a structured framework with standardised financial models, investment metrics, time-bound evaluation and approval workflows for consistent underwriting across outright acquisitions, joint developments and society redevelopment
- Governance of land investment: constituted a Land Investment Committee to review and recommend land investment proposals within the Board-approved framework, ensure due diligence and manage risk
- Broadbase the sales engine so bookings are not excessively dependent on new launches — sustenance bookings exceeded Rs. 600 Cr in FY25-26
- Deploy debt, kept comfortably within the Company's debt threshold, to fund extension into new markets
- Move design from project-level intent to organisation-wide, standardised design systems — standardised layouts, materials and pre-approved specifications to control cost while preserving premium experience, with a consistent design philosophy across Ahmedabad, Bengaluru and Mumbai
- Invest ahead of growth in leadership, execution capability and city-based teams so organisational capacity keeps pace with business growth
- Strengthen local sourcing networks in Bengaluru's high-growth corridors and marquee micro-markets to sustain a quality pipeline
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Arvind SmartSpaces' expansion is a land- and project-pipeline build-out rather than plant capex. In FY25-26 the Company added projects with an estimated cumulative topline potential of approximately Rs. 3,140 Cr: entry into Vadodara in Q2 with a horizontal township under the joint development model (~Rs. 700 Cr); in Q3 a premium residential high-rise in Vastrapur, Ahmedabad (~Rs. 400 Cr, 3.6 Lac sq ft) and a premium high-rise in Nallurahalli, Whitefield, Bengaluru (~Rs. 550 Cr, ~4.6 Lac sq ft); and in Q4 two more Bengaluru high-rises, at Sarjapur (~Rs. 860 Cr, ~6.8 Lac sq ft) and Nagondanahalli, Whitefield (~Rs. 330 Cr, ~2.5 Lac sq ft), plus its first Mumbai society redevelopment at Santacruz (~Rs. 300 Cr). Five of six acquisitions were high-rise residential, marking a deliberate deepening of the vertical portfolio alongside the Company's horizontal base. In MMR the Company expanded its redevelopment portfolio through Santacruz and Goregaon and announced a ~20 Mn Sq. Ft. horizontal township near Khopoli in the Mumbai 3.0 corridor; the MMR entry targets three opportunity segments — horizontal developments in emerging Mumbai 3.0 corridors, mid-sized redevelopment projects under-served by organised developers, and selective joint development across brownfield and greenfield locations. Management states the expansion strategy remains structurally asset-light, intending to maintain a 60-70% joint development mix over the medium term, complemented selectively by outright acquisitions where returns justify ownership, and expects to deploy meaningful capital toward business development over the coming years while preserving balance sheet flexibility. The Company is currently executing 16 projects through a mix of owned land, joint ventures and joint development agreements, and has delivered 16 projects to date. Funding: net borrowings of Rs. 31,302.96 Lakhs were availed during the year, with investments in new lands and projects funded out of strong business inflows and incremental borrowings; total standalone debt stood at Rs. 56,952.08 Lakhs as on March 31, 2026, and the consolidated net debt-to-equity ratio rose to 0.26 from (0.04) a year earlier. As the Company scales, it is investing in technology-led operational efficiency, including AI-enabled project management systems and construction technologies to improve execution predictability and timelines.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Indian real estate market size projected to grow from USD 580 Bn in 2026 to USD 1,210 Bn by 2032, a 13.04% CAGR, against an urban housing shortage of ~10 Mn units and a need for 30 Mn additional affordable homes by 2030
- Premiumisation: homes above Rs. 1 crore rose to 63% of total residential sales from 53% in 2024 and grew 6% y-o-y, while sub-Rs. 1 crore demand softened; premium housing contributed nearly 70% of new launches
- K-shaped consolidation toward branded and listed developers — large-cap listed developers held roughly 20% market share in FY25-26, up ~530 bps since FY20-21, with the top five accounting for nearly 60% of listed developers' pre-sales; management expects this to continue over the medium term
- Company-specific: record bookings, collections and unrecognised revenue of Rs. 3,733 Cr strengthen revenue visibility as projects move toward completion and handover
- Ahmedabad demand shifting up the price ladder (homes above Rs. 10 Mn at 25% of H2 2025 sales), with growth concentrated along the SG Highway and SP Ring Road corridor and metro connectivity toward GIFT City
- Bengaluru capital values up 12% y-o-y to Rs. 7,388 per sq ft with a decisive shift to premium inventory (Rs. 1.5-2.5 Cr segment at 45% of launches vs 24%), though inventory overhang rose to 13 months
- MMR sales running close to or ahead of launches, attributed by Anarock to genuine end-user demand rather than speculation; inventory overhang at 17 months, well below the 55-month 2020 peak
- Macro tailwinds: FY25-26 real GDP growth of 7.7%, CPI at 2.1% enabling 125 bps of cumulative rate cuts, repo rate at 5.25%, and Union Budget FY26-27 tax relief supporting discretionary spending and housing affordability
- Union Budget FY26-27 raises public capital expenditure and GST reform cut rates to 1% for affordable housing under construction, easing both developer economics and buyer affordability
- Management risk framing: elevated energy prices, subsidy pressure on government spending and uncertainty in global demand persist, though India's macroeconomic fundamentals remain strong; rising land and construction costs require greater design and procurement efficiency
- Unrecognised revenue of Rs. 3,733 Cr as at FY25-26, described as strengthening revenue visibility as projects move toward completion and handover
- Unrealised operating cash flows estimated at over Rs. 4,970 Crores over the next four to five years, based on the current project pipeline
- FY25-26 project additions with an estimated cumulative topline potential of approximately Rs. 3,140 Cr across Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Vadodara and MMR
- FY25-26 bookings of Rs. 1,550 Cr, of which new launches contributed nearly 60% (~Rs. 930 Cr) and sustenance bookings more than Rs. 600 Cr
- Q4 FY26 launches Arvind Skycrest (Bengaluru) and Arvind Greenfields (Vadodara) saw approximately 53% and 42% of launched inventory booked within a short period of launch
- Largest property redevelopment opportunity secured in Goregaon in April 2026 (post the reporting year)
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Arvind SmartSpaces is well-positioned to benefit from the growing demand for residential real estate in India, driven by its strong brand, execution capabilities, and strategic expansion across key growth markets. The company's focus on building a diversified portfolio, deepening city-level operating structures, and maintaining a disciplined approach to capital allocation will drive long-term growth and value creation for shareholders.

risks.note: Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk: 'The construction industry is prone to a high number of workplace injuries and accidents due to the nature of the work, which often involves heights and heavy machinery', with reputational risk if fair labour practices, human rights and employee health and safety are not ensured. Mitigation runs through the HIRA (Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment) framework, dedicated safety officers at active sites, regular training and tested emergency response plans; FY25-26 recorded a zero Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate, zero work-related injuries and zero fatalities. Because execution is largely outsourced to external contractors, the exposure sits partly outside direct control.
risks.risk: Workplace health, safety and labour-rights exposure at construction sites

risks.note: Flagged in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk with negative financial implications: 'Considering our dependency on water for the viability of our operations, we have identified it as a material risk'. Non-compliance with water regulations can result in fines and legal issues, and poor water management can damage local ecosystems. Mitigation is designed in at the project stage — water-efficient construction materials that need less curing water, recycling, rainwater harvesting and groundwater recharge.

Flagged in the BRSR material-issues table with negative financial implications: high emissions and inefficient energy use raise operating costs, poor practices can damage brand value, buyers are shifting toward green construction so laggards 'may lose competitive advantage and market share', and 'long term strategic risks include the potential for stricter future regulations and the need for costly retrofits or upgrades to meet these new standards'.
risks.risk: Emissions and energy management, including the risk of stricter future regulation

risks.note: The Directors' Report records net borrowings of Rs. 31,302.96 Lakhs availed during the year, with investments in new lands and projects funded out of business inflows and incremental borrowings, and total standalone debt of Rs. 56,952.08 Lakhs as on March 31, 2026. Land and business-development spend is front-loaded relative to project cash realisation, so an aggressive acquisition pace makes the balance sheet more sensitive to a slowdown in bookings or collections.
risks.risk: Rising leverage after a step-up in land and project investment

risks.note: New launches contributed nearly 60% of total FY26 bookings, approximately Rs. 930 Crores, and the two Q4 FY26 launches (Arvind Skycrest, Arvind Greenfields) drove a large share of the year's momentum. Bookings therefore depend on launches landing on schedule; approval, liaison or construction delays in a single large launch can move the whole year's pre-sales.
risks.risk: Dependence on a sustained new-launch cadence for bookings

risks.note: The Directors' Report notes that homes above Rs. 1 crore rose to 63% of residential sales while 'demand in the sub-Rs. 1 crore segment softened noticeably', with premium housing at nearly 70% of new launches. The Company's mid-to-premium positioning aligns with the strong end of the market but concentrates exposure in the segment where developers are collectively adding the most supply, and leaves it exposed if the premiumisation trend reverses.
risks.risk: Concentration of demand in the premium/mid-premium segment amid a softening mass market

risks.note: Management attributes the favourable operating environment partly to 'improving affordability through lower interest rates' after 125 basis points of cumulative rate cuts and a repo rate of 5.25%. Housing demand and the Company's own borrowing cost both move with the rate cycle, so a reversal would compress buyer affordability and project economics simultaneously.
risks.risk: Sensitivity to interest rates and housing affordability

risks.note: The MD&A flags risks that 'persist, particularly from elevated energy prices, subsidy pressures on government spending, and uncertainty in global demand', alongside a 9.88% rupee depreciation in FY25-26 (the steepest since FY11-12), a record Rs. 1.8 Trn of FPI outflows, an 8% fall in India's market capitalisation and continued West Asia conflict. Global growth is projected to slow to 3.0% in 2026 with global inflation rising to 4.7%.
